description: Width tiers for English Year 10 — all 25 descriptors across LA, LE and LY strands. Generated from ACARA v9 elaborations.
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor that satisfies the descriptor's command term. For concept/understanding descriptors (most LA, LE, LY): minimum engagement with one phenomenon, context or text example. For capability descriptors (LE08, LY06, LY07): minimum task context that genuinely meets the command term.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in the most common ACARA elaboration cases. What a well-taught Year 10 class would typically achieve. For concept descriptors: a range of contexts and examples that covers the descriptor's intended scope. For capability descriptors: a range of task types that develops the capability across the descriptor's full intent.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or task types — not harder versions of the same context. For concept standards: more cultural contexts, historical examples, cross-media comparisons. For capability standards: different task types, audiences, purposes or production contexts. First Nations Australian directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data for typical_width grounding and wider direction identification. Not treated as a required checklist — elaborations at similar specificity levels merged; sub-steps of the same activity treated as one item. First Nations elaborations always appear in wider.

AC9E10LA01.minimum_width: Identify at least two language alignment or distancing devices in a text and explain their intended effect on the audience.
AC9E10LA01.typical_width: Analyse a range of alignment and distancing devices, shared assumption appeals and inclusive/exclusive language across print and multimodal texts, explaining how each empowers or disempowers different audiences.
wider: Analyse alignment devices across texts from different political or cultural contexts, comparing how they function differently for different in-group audiences
Examine how First Nations Australian speakers or writers use pronoun and alignment strategies in advocacy or community contexts
Investigate how communities have reclaimed previously marginalising language as an act of empowerment and how that language shift reflects changing social power
elaborations: identifying language that seeks to align the listener or reader; for example, “of course”, “obviously”, “as you can imagine”
identifying the use of first person (“I”, “we”) and second person (“you”) pronouns to distance or involve the audience
identifying language used to reference or indicate shared assumptions
identifying language that appeals to shared cultural knowledge, values and beliefs
identifying examples of language that are inclusive or marginalising

AC9E10LA02.minimum_width: Identify one explicit evaluative statement and one implicit evaluative word or phrase in a text, explaining what value each reveals.
AC9E10LA02.typical_width: Analyse how evaluative language — both explicit and implicit — reveals values across a range of text types including reviews, opinion pieces and political texts, explaining what values are communicated and how.
wider: Compare explicit and implicit evaluative language across texts from different time periods or cultural contexts, examining how the values revealed differ
Examine how implicit evaluation in texts about First Nations Australians has reflected and reinforced colonial values, contrasted with contemporary First Nations-authored texts
Analyse how political language uses implicit evaluation to position audiences without making values explicit
elaborations: identifying explicit expressions of values when evaluating
identifying subtle or implied values communicated through language; for example, using a term such as “teenager” to refer to an individual rather than using a specific name

AC9E10LA03.minimum_width: Identify the main text structure and two language features in a text, describe their function, and make a supported judgement about whether they are effective in achieving the text's purpose.
AC9E10LA03.typical_width: Analyse text structures and language features across a range of text types (print, online, multimodal), evaluating the effectiveness of each in achieving its purpose with reasoned judgements and textual evidence.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of a print text transposed to an online environment, evaluating how the format change affects purpose achievement
Evaluate how documentaries or media reports achieve their purposes through combinations of graphics, text and sound
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors structure texts incorporating oral storytelling conventions and evaluate how effective those structures are for their intended audiences
elaborations: comparing the text structure and language features of a print text transposed to an online environment and evaluating the effectiveness of the online text
analysing the text structures and language features of reviews from different sources, and evaluating their effectiveness

analysing and experimenting with combinations of graphics, text and sound in the production of multimodal texts such as documentaries, media reports, online magazines and digital books to influence audience responses

AC9E10LA04.minimum_width: Identify one paragraph structure variation and one example of paragraph-image integration in texts and explain the effect or purpose of each.
AC9E10LA04.typical_width: Examine how paragraph structure is varied for cohesive and rhetorical effect across a range of text types, and how paragraphs and images are integrated across websites and graphic novels for different purposes.
wider: Compare image-text integration in graphic novels versus news websites, evaluating how the relationship between modes creates meaning differently in each
Examine how digital and online texts use unconventional paragraph structures to aid navigation and engagement
Analyse how First Nations Australian visual artists integrate text and image in community or activist publications
elaborations: examining how authors vary paragraph structures for effect
examining the integration of paragraphs and images on websites for effect
evaluating the effect of the integration of paragraphs and images in graphic novels

AC9E10LA05.minimum_width: Identify one deliberate sentence structure choice (e.g. passive voice, verbless clause) in a text and make a supported judgement about its effectiveness.
AC9E10LA05.typical_width: Identify and evaluate the effectiveness of a range of sentence structure choices — passive voice, verbless clauses, conjunction-opening sentences — across literary and non-literary texts.
wider: Compare how active versus passive constructions function in legal, scientific and journalistic texts, evaluating how each serves the text's purpose
Evaluate how authors' sentence structure choices shape characterisation or mood across different literary genres
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use sentence structure deliberately to assert voice or perspective
elaborations: recognising how the focus of a sentence can be changed through using the passive voice; for example, compare active “The police had caught the thief.” with passive “The thief had been caught.”
recognising how authors sometimes use verbless clauses for effect; for example, “And what about the other woman? With her dark glasses and briefcase.”
recognising that a sentence can begin with a coordinating conjunction for stylistic effect; for example, “And she went on planning how she would manage it.”

AC9E10LA06.minimum_width: Identify one nominalisation, one clause combination expressing a logical relation, and one abstract noun group in texts and explain how each achieves meaning or style.
AC9E10LA06.typical_width: Analyse how nominalisation, clause combination and noun group abstraction work across academic, journalistic and political texts to construct meaning and style, explaining what each syntactic choice achieves.
wider: Compare how nominalisation is used in scientific versus political texts, analysing how each uses nominalisation to construct authority or obscure agency
Examine how clause combinations in historical documents construct cause-effect relationships that shape interpretation of events
Analyse how abstract noun groups in philosophical or theoretical writing construct conceptual frameworks and enable generalisation
elaborations: considering how nominalisation affects the way in which events are constructed and explained, making some information more explicit than other information

analysing how logical relations between ideas are built up by combining independent with dependent clauses indicating cause, result, manner, concession, condition, and so on; for example, “Although the poet was not generally well received by critics during her life (concession), her reputation grew substantially after her death.”

considering how abstraction in a noun group allows for greater generalisation of complex ideas in a sentence; for example, “He focused on the political, religious, social and economic elements of the society in his thesis.”

AC9E10LA07.minimum_width: Identify two visual features in a still or moving image and evaluate how at least one creates nuance in a representation.
AC9E10LA07.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate how a range of visual features (lighting, angle, colour, framing) in still and moving images create nuanced representations, making supported judgements with visual evidence.
wider: Compare how the same visual features function differently in film, documentary and advertising contexts
Evaluate how documentary filmmakers use visual features to position audiences in relation to their subjects, examining ethical dimensions of those choices
Analyse how First Nations Australian visual artists use features such as light, colour and framing to challenge dominant visual conventions
elaborations: examining features of visual texts that create nuance in representations; for example, analysing the use of light and dark, and evaluating the impact of light and dark on representing duplicity

AC9E10LA08.minimum_width: Identify the meaning of at least two technical vocabulary terms and use them accurately in a short piece of analytical writing.
AC9E10LA08.typical_width: Identify and apply an expanding range of technical and academic vocabulary for literary, grammatical and rhetorical analysis with precision in academic writing.
wider: Compare technical vocabulary across literary criticism and film analysis, examining how field-specific terminology shapes analytical possibilities
Analyse how First Nations Australian scholars have developed or reclaimed technical vocabulary for analysing their literary and cultural traditions
Write analytical response on poetry using specific prosodic terminology (iambic pentameter, caesura, enjambment) and evaluate how vocabulary precision enables more exact analysis
elaborations: identifying the meaning of an increasing range of technical vocabulary; for example, using specific terms about rhythm such as “iambic pentameter” when analysing poetry
AC9E10LA08.width_notes: Limited width at the minimum tier — technical vocabulary use does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Wider directions extend through application in increasingly complex and domain-diverse texts.

AC9E10LA09.minimum_width: Identify one use of a specific punctuation mark (colon, semicolon, ellipsis) and one example of experimental or expressive punctuation in texts, explaining the effect of each.
AC9E10LA09.typical_width: Examine how authors use colons, semicolons, ellipses and expressive punctuation (multiple exclamation marks, unconventional marks) across expository and literary texts, explaining how each choice creates different effects.
wider: Compare how punctuation experimentation in poetry (e.g. Emily Dickinson's dashes) creates unique rhythm and meaning, and contrast with contemporary experimental writers
Examine how digital communication contexts have expanded expressive use of punctuation emojis and unconventional marks
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors use punctuation experimentally to represent oral speech patterns or cultural storytelling rhythms in print
elaborations: using colons and semicolons in expositions and other extended texts to add detail or extend an idea
examining an author’s use of ellipses to create tentativeness in a character’s speech
reviewing the use of punctuation to represent emotions; for example, the use of multiple exclamation marks or punctuation emojis

AC9E10LE01.minimum_width: Analyse how one individual or group is represented in a literary text and evaluate how that representation reflects the context of the text's production.
AC9E10LE01.typical_width: Analyse representations of individuals, groups and places across a literary text and evaluate how those representations reflect the social, cultural or historical context of the text, drawing on a range of First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.
wider: Compare representations of the same group (e.g. the anti-hero, the underdog) across texts from different authors and evaluate how each reflects its context differently
Analyse representations in texts by First Nations Australian authors who contemporise or modernise traditional stories and evaluate how they reflect contemporary context
Compare how humour is used to represent the underdog in Australian texts and evaluate what those representations reveal about Australian cultural context
elaborations: analysing the ways in which cultural stories may be retold and adapted across a range of contexts, such as the story of the “anti-hero”, and evaluating how the “anti-hero” reflects the context
analysing how stories written by First Nations Australian authors contemporise or modernise traditional stories and evaluating the responses of contemporary audiences
analysing how humour is used to represent the underdog in Australian texts and evaluating how the underdog reflects the context

AC9E10LE02.minimum_width: Identify another's interpretation of a text, reflect on how it compares with your own, and present one argument based on close textual analysis that extends the interpretation.
AC9E10LE02.typical_width: Engage with multiple interpretations of a literary text, present arguments based on close textual analysis to support and extend an interpretation, through an essay, director's notes or similar extended form.
wider: Debate whether a text possesses universal qualities, engaging with published critical perspectives and reflecting on how reader position shapes claims about universality
Examine critical responses to a First Nations Australian text from both First Nations and non-First Nations critics, reflecting on how reader position shapes interpretation
Research how a text's critical reception has changed over time and reflect on what changed interpretations reveal about shifting contexts
elaborations: debating whether a text possesses universal qualities and retains relevance
presenting arguments based on close textual analysis to support an interpretation of a text; for example, writing an essay or creating a set of director’s notes
creating personal reading lists in a variety of genres and explaining why texts qualify for inclusion on a particular list

AC9E10LE03.minimum_width: Identify one aesthetic quality in a text, trace it to a specific feature, and analyse how the context of the text's experience influences how the audience responds.
AC9E10LE03.typical_width: Analyse how aesthetic qualities associated with text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features, and the context of experience, combine to influence audience response.
wider: Compare the aesthetic qualities of texts experienced in different modes (read silently, read aloud, set to music) and analyse how mode of experience affects aesthetic response
Examine how the context of audience (First Nations versus non-First Nations readers) shapes response to First Nations Australian texts differently
Compare audience responses to a text in its original context and in a contemporary context, analysing how time and cultural shift affect response
elaborations: examining a range of texts and evaluating the effect of text structures and language features; for example, determining whether the narrative position of a child evokes reader sympathy towards an event or issue

AC9E10LE04.minimum_width: Identify one ethical position in a literary text and evaluate its strengths and weaknesses with supporting analysis.
AC9E10LE04.typical_width: Evaluate ethical positions and world views across literary texts from a range of cultural, historical and social contexts, making supported judgements about what each text challenges, reinforces or privileges.
wider: Evaluate conflicting ethical positions presented across two literary texts from different cultural contexts on the same issue, making a reasoned comparative assessment
Examine a significant ethical issue treated in First Nations Australian literature and evaluate the position(s) the text takes, considering the cultural and political context
Evaluate how the same ethical position is treated differently across texts from different time periods, assessing what each treatment reveals about its historical moment
elaborations: identifying and analysing ethical positions on a significant issue, including values and/or principles involved, and evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of the position presented

AC9E10LE05.minimum_width: Identify at least two language devices that layer meaning in a text and one intertextual connection, and analyse how each shapes interpretation.
AC9E10LE05.typical_width: Analyse how text structure, language features, literary devices and intertextual connections combine to shape interpretations of texts across poetry, short stories or novel/film extracts.
wider: Examine how satirical texts use intertextual references to shape interpretation and what happens to interpretation when readers lack the referenced knowledge
Analyse how First Nations Australian literary texts create intertextual connections to traditional narratives and evaluate how those connections shape meaning differently for different readers
Compare how two texts that reference the same canonical source use that intertextual connection for different interpretive purposes
elaborations: examining a range of short poems, a short story, or extracts from a novel or film to find and discuss examples of how language devices layer meaning and influence the responses of listeners, viewers or readers
examining satirical representations of events or ideas and determining how satire shapes interpretations and responses

AC9E10LE06.minimum_width: Identify how voice is constructed in two different text types and evaluate how each evokes a different emotional response.
AC9E10LE06.typical_width: Compare and evaluate how voice as a literary device is constructed and used across poetry, novels and film to evoke different emotional responses, making supported judgements with textual evidence.
wider: Compare the voice of protest across a range of poems or songs and evaluate how different voices evoke a response from different audiences
Evaluate how voice in a film creates a different emotional response than the same story told through prose, analysing what the medium change does to the voice
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use voice across text types to evoke emotional responses that challenge or illuminate dominant perspectives
elaborations: comparing the “voice” of protest in a range of poems or songs and evaluating how different voices evoke a response

AC9E10LE07.minimum_width: Identify at least two aesthetic qualities using appropriate literary analysis terms and evaluate the use and effect of at least one literary device.
AC9E10LE07.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate the aesthetic qualities of a literary text using a range of literary analysis terms, making supported judgements about multiple literary devices and their contribution to the text's overall aesthetic effect.
wider: Evaluate how an author's aesthetic choices create a distinctive style, comparing with other authors' approaches to the same genre or form
Evaluate the aesthetic qualities of a First Nations Australian text on its own terms, considering the aesthetic traditions from which it draws
Write a published-style review of a literary text that evaluates aesthetic qualities for a specific audience
elaborations: using terms associated with literary text analysis; for example, “stanza”, “figurative language”, “symbolism” and “soundtrack”, when evaluating aspects that are valued and that contain aesthetic qualities
analysing and evaluating the use of literary devices; for example, commenting on the effect of symbolism in a text

AC9E10LE08.minimum_width: Create a literary text with a consistent voice, at least two deliberate structural or device choices, and evidence of editing with stated reasons for revisions.
AC9E10LE08.typical_width: Create, edit and reflect on a literary text with a sustained voice, selecting and adapting text structures, literary devices, and language and visual features for a specific purpose and audience.
wider: Create a suite of short texts on the same key idea expressed in different voices, comparing how voice shapes what can be said and how
Experiment with aesthetic features from mentor texts in own literary writing, with reflection on what was borrowed and how it was adapted
Create a literary text that incorporates or responds to a First Nations Australian text, with reflection on the choices required to do so responsibly
elaborations: experimenting with the aesthetic features that authors use in their own texts
creating a range of texts, experimenting with and manipulating “voice” for particular purposes and audiences
creating and editing a suite of short texts that focus on a key idea expressed in different voices
describing choices of text structures, literary devices, language, auditory or visual features made in a literary text and reflecting on the effect of those choices

AC9E10LY01.minimum_width: Analyse how one person, place, event or concept is represented in a text and evaluate how that representation reflects the context of its production.
AC9E10LY01.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate how people, places, events and concepts are represented across a range of texts, making supported judgements about how context shapes those representations.
wider: Compare how stereotypes of people, places or events are constructed across a range of texts and evaluate the assumptions underlying each
Analyse representations of events and issues in First Nations Australian media, examining how representations differ from mainstream media
Evaluate how representations of First Nations Australians in Australian media have changed over time and assess what those changes reveal about shifting contexts
elaborations: evaluating stereotypes of people, places, events and concepts, and expressing opinions on these representations in the contexts for which they are created
analysing representations of events and issues in First Nations Australian media

AC9E10LY02.minimum_width: Identify one text structure feature and one language feature in a spoken text, explain their effects, and present an opinion about the text using interaction skills.
AC9E10LY02.typical_width: Analyse the purposes and effects of text structures and language features in spoken and multimodal media texts, and use interaction skills to discuss and present a developed opinion.
wider: Compare spoken text features across different genres (interview, documentary, political speech) and analyse how genre shapes structure and language choices
Examine how spoken features of First Nations Australian storytelling or oratory function differently from Western speech conventions
Participate in a structured discussion where multiple opinions about a spoken text are presented and debated, using interaction skills to build on and respond to others
elaborations: analysing spoken and multimodal features of media texts and discussing the effects of these features; for example, presenting an opinion on the combination of words and sound in creating mood

AC9E10LY03.minimum_width: Identify one language feature that explicitly represents a value and one that implicitly represents a value, and evaluate the significance of each.
AC9E10LY03.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate how language features across a range of texts represent values, beliefs and attitudes both implicitly and explicitly, making supported judgements about the significance of the representations.
wider: Analyse social or political cartoons to identify the implicit and explicit values, beliefs and attitudes expressed through visual and language features
Evaluate how values represented in media texts about First Nations Australian communities have changed over time
Compare how different texts covering the same event represent values differently and assess what that reveals about the values of the text producers
elaborations: analysing social or political cartoons to identify the implicit and explicit values, beliefs and attitudes expressed

AC9E10LY04.minimum_width: Identify how ideas are organised in a text and evaluate whether the organisation is effective in achieving its purpose.
AC9E10LY04.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate how authors organise ideas in a range of texts — print, digital and multimodal — making supported judgements about how organisation achieves purpose.
wider: Compare how ideas are organised in texts designed for different platforms (print versus webpage) and analyse how the platform shapes organisational choices
Compare the organisation of ideas in political pamphlets and evaluate the impact of each in achieving its persuasive purpose
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors organise ideas in ways that reflect non-linear or culturally specific narrative or argumentative structures
elaborations: identifying the organisation of ideas in a text and determining the purpose and effect; for example, how the eye is drawn across or down a webpage for a purpose
evaluating how ideas in an online review are organised and its success in achieving its purpose
comparing the organisation of ideas in political pamphlets and determining the impact of each

AC9E10LY05.minimum_width: Apply at least two comprehension strategies to analyse a complex idea in a text and produce a supported interpretation.
AC9E10LY05.typical_width: Integrate comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning and inferring — to analyse and interpret complex and abstract ideas across different text types.
wider: Interpret the representation of an abstract concept (e.g. justice, belonging) by integrating comprehension strategies across multiple texts
Apply integrated comprehension strategies to interpret abstract concepts in First Nations Australian texts, considering how cultural knowledge shapes the connecting strategy
Use integrated strategies to interpret how a character archetype functions across different cultural contexts, analysing what the archetype's variation reveals
elaborations: monitoring the language features associated with right and wrong in a text and interpreting the representation of the abstract concept of justice
interpreting how visual features represent abstract concepts in advertising, such as the representation of parenthood in advertisements
summarising the qualities and interpreting the role of a character archetype in a range of texts and analysing the importance of this archetype

AC9E10LY06.minimum_width: Plan, create and edit a written text with at least two deliberate structural or language feature choices for a specific purpose and audience, with a reflection on choices made.
AC9E10LY06.typical_width: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts that organise, expand and develop ideas through deliberate experimentation with text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features for specific purposes and audiences.
wider: Design a webpage that combines navigation, text, sound, and moving and still images for a specific audience, making deliberate structural choices about how the modes work together
Create a written text that compels readers to empathise with the ideas and emotions expressed or implied
Publish a final text to a real audience (school publication, competition) and reflect on how the publishing context shaped final editing decisions
elaborations: presenting a structured argument by providing a statement of the major arguments or concerns relating to an issue, previewing the structure of arguments, structuring the text to provide a major point for each paragraph with succinct elaboration, and concluding with a summary of the main issues or recommendations in an argument
creating written and multimodal texts that compel readers to empathise with the ideas and emotions expressed or implied
designing a webpage that combines navigation, text, sound, and moving and still images for a specific audience

reviewing, editing and refining their own and others’ texts for accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation, and to achieve particular purposes and address specific audiences through control and organisation of content, sentence structures, vocabulary choices and visual features
reflecting on the effect of choices made in a written or multimodal text and how these choices may be changed or developed in future texts

AC9E10LY07.minimum_width: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver a spoken presentation using at least two rhetorical devices, with evidence of rehearsal in delivery.
AC9E10LY07.typical_width: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that experiment with rhetorical devices and the organisation and development of ideas to engage audiences for different purposes.
wider: Create and deliver a persuasive multimodal presentation that manipulates rhetorical devices to compel listeners to act
Participate in debates or panel discussions about issues related to a text, using interaction and rhetorical skills responsively
Deliver a reflective character monologue that integrates rhetorical performance with analytical insight about the character's choices
elaborations: taking the role of a character in a reflective monologue, and considering and justifying actions and choices at a critical moment in the text
creating spoken multimodal texts that manipulate rhetorical devices to compel listeners to act
discussing and negotiating with peers in debates and panel discussions about issues related to a text

AC9E10LY08.minimum_width: Accurately spell technical vocabulary in context and identify one deliberate spelling manipulation in a text, explaining the effect it creates.
AC9E10LY08.typical_width: Use knowledge of the spelling system to spell words accurately across a range of registers and text types, and identify and explain deliberate spelling manipulation across literary, advertising and digital text contexts.
wider: Examine how homophones and deliberate misspellings are used in advertising and brand naming and evaluate their effectiveness
Analyse how spelling manipulation is used in digital communication contexts to create new meaning or group identity
Examine how authors use spelling manipulation to represent dialect or accent and evaluate the ethics of such representations for different communities
elaborations: using homophones to create new spelling of familiar words; for example, “lite milk”
